text: omas (p.657). MALIGNANT NEOPLASMS OF THE OESOPHAGUS. Oesophageal cancer has perhaps the greatest variation in incidence between different geographical regions of any cancer, and is endemic in many parts of the world. The two major histological types are squamous cell car- cinoma and adenocarcinoma.1-3 Squamous cell carcino- ma is strongly associated with tobacco and alcohol use, and may occur as a second primary tumour in patients with tumours of the upper aerodigestive tract (see Ma- lignant Neoplasms of the Head and Neck, below). Ade- nocarcinoma is more common in non-endemic regions, including many developed countries,2 and is associated with Barrett’s oesophagus (see Gastro-oesophageal Re- flux Disease, p.1696). Oesophageal cancer usually de- velops as a growth or ulcerative lesion of the oesopha- gus with extensive infiltration of the mucosa and invasion of neighbouring structures. Lymphatic and blood-borne metastasis occurs at a relatively early stage. Symptoms of pain and dysphagia due to obstruc- tion occur late, and overall, more than half of all pa- tients have unresectable or metastatic disease at initial presentation. Metastatic disease is associated with a median survival of less than 1 year.1 Patients with stages I to III disease may be offered either surgical resection or a combination of chemotherapy (with cisplatin and fluorouracil) and radiotherapy.2-4 Surgical patients who are node-positive, or otherwise considered to be at higher risk, may be given postoperative chemothera- py with radiotherapy.2 The 5-year survival rate varies with the stage of the disease at initial presentation, from about 50 to 80% in the few with stage I disease, to 10 to 15% in those with stage III disease.1 In consequence, there has been great interest in adjuvant treatment (pre-operative or postoperative).5 There is no clear evidence that pre-operative radiotherapy alone improves survival.1,3,6 However, there has been con- flicting evidence on the value of chemoradiotherapy or chemotherapy used before surgery, with some trials show- ing improved survival, and others no additional benefit.1,3 A systematic review7 found that pre-operative chemoradi- otherapy significantly improved the 3-year mortality rates compared with surgery alone, and a later meta-analysis8 found a significant survival benefit for neoadjuvant chem- oradiotherapy (versus surgery alone) in patients with oesophageal adenocarcinoma or squamous cell carcino- ma.
